sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Jaintia Rebellion (1860-1863)**: Primarily a reaction against the imposition of the **Income Tax** (1860) and the **House Tax** on the Jaintia people, which violated their traditional autonomy.
• **Garo Rebellion (1872-1873)**: Triggered by the British attempt to establish a direct administrative link between the **Garo Hills** and the plains, coupled with the encroachment of zamindars and British surveyors.
• **Socio-Political Catalyst**: The British policy of 'non-interference' was abandoned in favor of 'direct control' to secure the frontier against Burmese and tribal raids.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The transition from 'tributary status' to 'direct taxation' served as the primary trigger for both movements.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya); Led by U Kiang Nangbah.
Imposition of Income Tax; interference in religious/social customs.
Symbol of tribal resistance against fiscal imperialism.
Garo Hills (Meghalaya); Resistance against British surveyors.
Fear of annexation; encroachment on traditional land rights.
Led to the 'Garo Hills Act of 1869' and subsequent pacification.

items.definition: The iconic leader of the Jaintia rebellion; executed by the British in 1862. He is a symbol of Jaintia nationalism.
A colonial fiscal instrument used to assert sovereignty over tribal territories; often perceived as a direct challenge to tribal sovereignty.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Administrative Consolidation**: Post-rebellion, the British implemented the 'Scheduled Districts Act' to isolate tribal areas from general administration.
• **Frontier Policy**: Shifted from 'Forward Policy' to 'Closed Border Policy' to minimize administrative costs.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Lack of unified tribal leadership; superior British military technology (Enfield rifles vs. traditional weapons).
• **Solutions**: Integration of tribal rights into the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution as a historical corrective.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'J-I-G' (Jaintia-Income-Garo).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Jaintia rebellion was triggered by Income tax; Garo rebellion was about land/surveying.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the Jaintia rebellion with the Khasi rebellion. Remember: Jaintia = Income Tax; Khasi = Road construction/British encroachment.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Fiscal Imperialism' to describe the British imposition of taxes on tribal societies that operated on a barter or non-monetary economy.

keyTakeaways: Tribal movements in the North-East were primarily defensive, aiming to preserve traditional autonomy.
The transition from 'tribute' to 'tax' was the single most important factor for tribal unrest.
Post-rebellion, the British adopted a policy of 'Excluded Areas' to prevent further unrest, which influenced the Sixth Schedule.
